stemMd: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Why does it normally become turgid rather than burst?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Its chloroplasts pump all incoming water out.

options.label: B
options.textMd: It immediately loses all its solutes.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Its cell wall resists expansion as water enters.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Pure water has no effect on plant cells.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Its membrane is completely impermeable to water.

explanationMd: Water enters because the cell contents contain dissolved substances. As the protoplast presses against the cell wall, wall resistance produces turgor pressure, opposing further net entry. The wall is a mechanical constraint; the plasma membrane is still permeable to water.

distractorRationale.e: Water does cross the membrane and enters under these conditions.
distractorRationale.b: Solute loss is not the normal explanation for turgor.
distractorRationale.a: Chloroplasts do not serve as pumps for this purpose.
distractorRationale.d: Pure water usually drives water entry into the cell.
